claims: Bystolic treats hypertension alone or with other antihypertensives. Blood-pressure lowering reduces cardiovascular risk across antihypertensive classes, but the label states no controlled trials demonstrate cardiovascular-event reduction specifically with Bystolic. The label does not approve treatment of angina, acute/recent MI or heart failure; its older heart-failure study is not an approval or preferred-treatment claim.

claims: Most adults with hypertension
5 mg orally once daily, with or without food. Increase at 2-week intervals if needed, up to 40 mg/day. More frequent dosing is unlikely to help.
Severe renal impairment
CrCl <30 mL/min: start 2.5 mg once daily; increase slowly. Dialysis has not been studied.
Moderate hepatic impairment
Start 2.5 mg once daily; increase slowly. Severe impairment, Child-Pugh >B, is contraindicated.
Older patients / CYP2D6 poor metabolizers
No routine dose adjustment solely for age or poor-metabolizer genotype; assess individual response and comorbidities.

claims: When planned discontinuation is appropriate, taper over 1–2 weeks when possible with prescriber observation and minimized physical activity; abrupt withdrawal can cause angina, MI or ventricular arrhythmia. Worsening angina/acute coronary insufficiency requires prompt clinician reassessment and possible temporary restart. Full PI section 17 advises taking only the next scheduled dose after a missed dose; appended patient leaflet says take when remembered unless close to next. These differ: obtain exact-package pharmacist instructions and never double; no universal catch-up dose is inferred.
Avoid abrupt interruption, even without known coronary disease. Recent MI and angina were not studied. Decompensated cardiac failure is contraindicated; reassess worsening heart-failure symptoms.
Patients with bronchospastic disease generally should not receive beta blockers. Nebivolol can aggravate peripheral arterial insufficiency and can cause bradycardia, hypotension or AV block.

Beta blockers may mask tachycardia from hypoglycemia and increase severe/prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with diabetes, fasting or vomiting. Severe hypoglycemia needs emergency care. They can mask thyrotoxicosis; abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm.

Inform anesthesia teams: ongoing beta-blocker treatment generally continues perioperatively with appropriate monitoring; do not independently stop before surgery. Myocardial-depressing anesthetics increase risk.

Severe allergy reactions may be greater and less responsive to usual epinephrine doses. Known/suspected pheochromocytoma requires alpha blockade before beta blockade. Renal/hepatic impairment and CYP2D6 inhibitors can increase exposure.

Severe bradycardia; heart block greater than first degree; cardiogenic shock; decompensated cardiac failure; sick sinus syndrome unless a permanent pacemaker is present; severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >B); or hypersensitivity to components.
The selected Bystolic label has no boxed warning. Its abrupt-cessation warning still describes potentially serious coronary events.

Reported trial reactions include headache, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, diarrhea, bradycardia and edema. Postmarketing reports include AV block, hypotension/syncope, bronchospasm, acute pulmonary edema/renal failure and hypersensitivity; frequency/causality cannot be reliably estimated. Overdose can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, heart failure, hypoglycemia, bronchospasm or heart block: obtain immediate Poison Help/emergency assessment and monitored supportive treatment. Hemodialysis is not expected to enhance clearance because protein binding is high; do not use label overdose measures as a home protocol.
Other beta blockers
Do not combine.
CYP2D6 inhibitors
Examples: fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, propafenone. Use caution, monitor response; nebivolol dose may need reduction. No universal percentage reduction is supplied.
Verapamil / diltiazem / disopyramide
Additive myocardial depression and AV slowing. Monitor ECG and blood pressure.
Digoxin / digitalis glycosides
Additive AV slowing and bradycardia, despite no major PK change in the label study.
Reserpine / guanethidine
Closely monitor for excessive sympathetic suppression.
Clonidine withdrawal
Prescriber-directed sequence: discontinue Bystolic for several days before gradual clonidine taper; reconcile with safe beta-blocker withdrawal.

Other pressure-lowering drugs can add hypotension even when no pharmacokinetic interaction was found. Review OTC medicines and prescriptions before adding therapy; clinically titrate rather than equate absence of PK changes with absence of pharmacodynamic risk.

Start 2.5 mg/day for CrCl <30 or moderate hepatic impairment, with slow escalation. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >B) is contraindicated; dialysis data are absent. Older age alone requires no label dose change, but comorbid renal/hepatic disease, conduction problems and co-medications still need review.

Human pregnancy data are insufficient to define developmental risk, and untreated hypertension also poses maternal/fetal risks. Third-trimester beta-blocker exposure can cause neonatal hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycemia or respiratory depression; observe newborns accordingly. Human milk data are absent; because beta blockers may seriously affect nursing infants, Bystolic is not recommended during breastfeeding. Discuss an appropriate hypertension plan rather than abruptly withdraw treatment.

Pediatric safety/effectiveness is unestablished; selected patient leaflet states not approved below 18. Do not convert juvenile animal findings into a clinical pediatric dose. Decompensated failure is contraindicated; an older chronic-HF trial in patients over 70 does not establish a U.S. HF indication or a full HF treatment regimen.

Nebivolol preferentially blocks beta1 receptors in extensive metabolizers at doses ≤10 mg; poor metabolizers and higher doses have beta1 and beta2 blockade. It lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and clinically relevant alpha1 blockade. Possible antihypertensive contributors include slower heart rate, reduced contractility/renin/sympathetic outflow and vasodilation; the exact response mechanism is not settled.

Peak plasma levels occur about 1.5–4 hours after dosing; food does not change relevant PK. Protein binding is about 98%. Glucuronidation and CYP2D6 oxidation produce active metabolites. Effective d-nebivolol half-life is about 12 hours in extensive and 19 hours in poor metabolizers; higher parent exposure in poor metabolizers does not alone mandate dose adjustment. Moderate liver/severe renal impairment lowers clearance; assess response and toxicity.

Follow blood pressure, pulse, dizziness/syncope and heart-failure signs during titration. ECG monitoring is needed with verapamil/diltiazem-type combinations; assess renal/hepatic status and CYP2D6 interactions. Monitor for hypoglycemia by symptoms other than tachycardia when diabetes, fasting or vomiting is present. No universal lab-frequency or home pulse stop-threshold is supplied.

Take daily as prescribed, with or without food. Do not stop or double after a missed dose; ask pharmacist to reconcile the two label instructions. Report breathing difficulty, rapid weight gain/edema, fainting or excessive slowing. Learn individual effects before driving; tell surgical teams and discuss pregnancy/breastfeeding before treatment changes.

Store 20–25°C. Dispense in tight, light-resistant container with child-resistant closure. Keep out of children’s reach and retain exact-package patient instructions; no unsupported refrigeration or splitting instruction is supplied.

An oral beta-adrenergic blocker for hypertension. This profile follows the selected current Bystolic label, including renal/hepatic starting doses, conduction risk, CYP2D6 interactions and supervised withdrawal.

Do not stop nebivolol suddenly. Marked bradycardia, fainting, breathing difficulty or worsening edema/weight gain require clinical assessment. Severe liver impairment and decompensated cardiac failure are contraindications; renal impairment and interacting drugs can increase exposure.
Therapeutic class
Beta-adrenergic blocker
Representative formulation
Bystolic 5 mg oral tablet
Usual adult start
5 mg once daily · individualize

gaps.resolution: Both disclosed; pharmacist exact-package reconciliation, never double; no unqualified catch-up directive.
Hypertension only; no controlled Bystolic event-reduction trial; HF trial and class BP benefit not represented as own approved HF/MI outcomes.

Severe hepatic Child-Pugh>B contraindication maintained despite dose paragraph not-recommended wording; dialysis/pediatric unestablished. CYP2D6 poor metabolizer no automatic dose adjustment distinguished from inhibitors.
